reader.summary: Iraqi courts handed down life sentences to six or seven French citizens convicted of Islamic State membership, a case that drew heavy international coverage and marked a significant judicial milestone. The Tishreen protest movement marked its seventh anniversary with reform demands and a symbolic 'wall of wishes' honoring slain protesters from 2019. The Pope visited Mosul, releasing a dove and praying for the dead, while Iraq's Christian community reflected on what was described as a bittersweet first Christmas home after the Islamic State. In diplomacy, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi made a historic visit to Syria to meet Ahmed al-Sharaa, signaling a new phase in bilateral relations. A separate court sentenced two politicians and an oil official in a graft case. On the security front, a drone was intercepted near Baghdad's Green Zone, and PKK-linked Yazidi militia units agreed to disarm and integrate into the national army. Economically, the United States permitted wind-down transactions with an Iran-linked Iraqi bank, and Norway's DNO explored exporting Kurdish oil via Syria. The week combined judicial closure on a high-profile case with diplomatic outreach and modest security and economic moves.

display.eli5:
Iraq just handed life sentences to a group of French citizens who were members of the Islamic State group. This is a big deal because France is now dealing with the aftermath. Its government will react diplomatically, the families will file appeals, and it will be a talking point in French politics for weeks to come.

At the same time, Iraq's prime minister just made a historic trip to Syria to meet the new leader there. That visit opens the door to real agreements between the two countries, like trade routes or border arrangements, and we should see the first concrete deal announced in the coming days.

On the security side, a group of Yazidi fighters linked to the Kurdish PKK militia agreed to hand in their weapons and join the national army. The first units will start this process at checkpoints, and other armed groups will be watching closely to see if this works.

A surprise would be if the seventh anniversary of the 2019 Tishreen protests, where Iraqis demanded government reforms, turns into a new march or sit-in rather than just a symbolic memorial wall. That would signal the frustration has not gone away after all these years.
